concepts: Powers of complex numbers (De Moivre's theorem)
Quadratic equation from its roots
questions.question: Let $p,q\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\left(1-\sqrt3 i\right)^{200}=2^{199}(p+iq)$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Then $p+q+q^2$ and $p-q+q^2$ are roots of the equation:
questions.key_idea: Write $1-\sqrt3 i$ in polar form so that the 200th power only needs the exponent reduced modulo $2\pi$.
solution: Sum of the roots $=4$ and product $=(2-\sqrt3)(2+\sqrt3)=1$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's solution begins with $(1+\sqrt3 i)^{200}$ although the question has $(1-\sqrt3 i)^{200}$, and so gets $p=-1,\ q=\sqrt3$. The correct values are $p=-1,\ q=-\sqrt3$ (the sign of $q$ flips). The two roots $2\pm\sqrt3$ are only interchanged, so the answer (B) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $1-\sqrt3 i=-2\omega$ with $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$, so the power reduces through $\omega^3=1$.
solution: Only $q^2=3$ and the value $p=-1$ matter: the roots are $p+q^2\pm q=2\pm\sqrt3$, with sum 4 and product 1, so $x^2-4x+1=0$.

useful_results: $1+\sqrt3 i=-2\omega^2$ and $1-\sqrt3 i=-2\omega$ where $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$; so $(1\pm\sqrt3 i)^n=(-2)^n\omega^{\pm n}$ and only $n \bmod 3$ matters.
$\left(1+\sqrt3 i\right)^n+\left(1-\sqrt3 i\right)^n=2^{n+1}\cos\frac{n\pi}{3}$ (check $n=2$: $(-2+2\sqrt3i)+(-2-2\sqrt3 i)=-4=2^3\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}$).
The roots $p+q^2\pm q$ differ only in the sign of $q$: their sum is $2(p+q^2)$ and their product is $(p+q^2)^2-q^2$, so only $q^2$ and $p$ are needed.

concepts: Modulus, conjugate and polar form of a complex number
questions.question: The value of $\left(\frac{1+\sin\frac{2\pi}{9}+i\cos\frac{2\pi}{9}}{1+\sin\frac{2\pi}{9}-i\cos\frac{2\pi}{9}}\right)^3$ is:
questions.key_idea: For $|z|=1$ we have $\bar z=\frac1z$, so $\frac{1+z}{1+\bar z}=z$ and the cube is just $z^3$.
solution: Let $z=\sin\frac{2\pi}{9}+i\cos\frac{2\pi}{9}$; then $|z|=1$, so $\bar z=\frac1z$ and the denominator is $1+\bar z$.
$\frac{1+z}{1+\bar z}=\frac{1+z}{1+\frac1z}=z$, so the required value is $z^3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the number as $e^{i\varphi}$ and use the half-angle factorisation $1+e^{i\varphi}=2\cos\frac\varphi2\,e^{i\varphi/2}$.
solution: Dividing, the ratio is $e^{i\varphi}$ (the common real factor $2\cos\frac\varphi2\ne0$ cancels).

useful_results: For $|z|=1$: $\frac{1+z}{1+\bar z}=z$; in general $\frac{1+e^{i\varphi}}{1+e^{-i\varphi}}=e^{i\varphi}$ for any real $\varphi$ with $\cos\frac\varphi2\ne0$.
$\sin\theta+i\cos\theta=ie^{-i\theta}=e^{i(\pi/2-\theta)}$: swapping sine and cosine reflects the angle about $\frac\pi4$.
$1+e^{i\varphi}=2\cos\frac\varphi2\,e^{i\varphi/2}$ and $1-e^{i\varphi}=-2i\sin\frac\varphi2\,e^{i\varphi/2}$ - the standard half-angle factorisations.

concepts: Locus of a complex number (straight line)
questions.question: Let $z_1=2+3i$ and $z_2=3+4i$. The set $S=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-z_1|^2-|z-z_2|^2=|z_1-z_2|^2\right\}$ represents a:
options: straight line with the sum of its intercepts on the coordinate axes equals $-18$
straight line with the sum of its intercepts on the coordinate axes equals $14$
hyperbola with the length of the transverse axis $7$
questions.answer: (C) straight line with the sum of its intercepts on the coordinate axes equal to $14$
questions.key_idea: The squares $x^2+y^2$ cancel in the difference, so the locus is a straight line.
solution: $x+y=7$: a straight line, so the hyperbola options (B), (D) are rejected.
Intercepts: $7$ on the $x$-axis and $7$ on the $y$-axis; their sum is $14$, option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: $z_2$ lies on the locus and the locus is perpendicular to the line $z_1z_2$, so the line is fixed without any expansion.
solution: The $x^2+y^2$ terms cancel, so the locus is a line; it is perpendicular to $z_1z_2$ (the difference of squared distances changes only along that direction).
The direction of $z_1z_2$ is $(1,1)$, so the locus has slope $-1$ and passes through $(3,4)$: $x+y=7$.
The intercepts are $7$ and $7$; the sum is $14$, option (C).

useful_results: $|z-a|^2-|z-b|^2=k$ is always a straight line perpendicular to the segment $ab$ (the quadratic terms cancel); $k=0$ gives the perpendicular bisector.
With $k=|a-b|^2$ the line passes through $b$; with $k=-|a-b|^2$ it passes through $a$.
By contrast $|z-a|^2+|z-b|^2=|a-b|^2$ is the circle on $ab$ as diameter (Pythagoras / Thales); $|z-a|=k|z-b|$ with $k\ne1$ is a circle.

concepts: Locus of a complex number (circle of Apollonius)
questions.question: Let $z$ be a complex number such that $\left|\frac{z-2i}{z+i}\right|=2$, $z\neq-i$. Then $z$ lies on the circle of radius $2$ and centre:
questions.key_idea: A constant ratio of distances $\ne1$ is a circle; square the modulus and use $|w|^2=w\bar w$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The ends of a diameter of an Apollonius circle divide the segment joining the two fixed points internally and externally in the ratio $2:1$.
solution: Fixed points $A=2i$ and $B=-i$; the locus is $PA=2PB$.
$P_1P_2$ is a diameter: centre $\frac{0-4i}{2}=-2i$, i.e. $(0,-2)$; radius $\frac{4}{2}=2$, which agrees with the given radius. Option (B).

useful_results: $|z-a|=k|z-b|$ ($k\ne1$): diameter ends divide $ab$ in the ratio $k:1$ internally and externally; centre $\frac{a-k^2b}{1-k^2}$, radius $\frac{k|a-b|}{|1-k^2|}$ (here $\frac{2i+4i}{-3}=-2i$ and $\frac{2\cdot3}{3}=2$).
For $k=1$ the locus is the perpendicular bisector of $ab$.
Sanity check: the ratio $\frac{|z-A|}{|z-B|}$ is $\infty$ at $B$, so the circle must enclose $B=-i$ and exclude $A=2i$; $|{-i}-(-2i)|=1<2$ and $|2i-(-2i)|=4>2$ confirm this.

concepts: Real and imaginary parts of complex numbers
questions.question:
For two non-zero complex numbers $z_1$ and $z_2$, if $\mathrm{Re}(z_1z_2)=0$ and $\mathrm{Re}(z_1+z_2)=0$, then which of the following are possible?
A. $\mathrm{Im}(z_1)>0$ and $\mathrm{Im}(z_2)>0$
B. $\mathrm{Im}(z_1)<0$ and $\mathrm{Im}(z_2)>0$
C. $\mathrm{Im}(z_1)>0$ and $\mathrm{Im}(z_2)<0$
D. $\mathrm{Im}(z_1)<0$ and $\mathrm{Im}(z_2)<0$
questions.key_idea: The two conditions give $y_1y_2=-x_1^2<0$, so the imaginary parts have opposite signs.
solution: $x_1\neq0$: if $x_1=0$ then $x_2=0$ and (i) gives $y_1y_2=0$, so one of $z_1,z_2$ would be $0$, which is excluded.
So B and C are possible while A and D are impossible; option (A) 'B and C'. (Example: $z_1=1+i$, $z_2=-1-i$.)
questions.correction_note: The PDF goes from $y_1y_2=-x_1^2$ straight to 'opposite signs'. That needs $x_1\neq0$ (otherwise $y_1y_2=0$ and one number would be $0$). Added this step; the answer is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Polar form: the argument condition from $\mathrm{Re}(z_1z_2)=0$ and the sign pattern of the cosines from $\mathrm{Re}(z_1+z_2)=0$ cannot both hold when the imaginary parts have the same sign.
solution: Suppose both imaginary parts are positive: $\theta_1,\theta_2\in(0,\pi)$, so $\theta_1+\theta_2\in(0,2\pi)$ and equals $\frac\pi2$ or $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.
If $\theta_1+\theta_2=\frac\pi2$ then both angles lie in $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, so $\cos\theta_1,\cos\theta_2>0$ and $\mathrm{Re}(z_1+z_2)=r_1\cos\theta_1+r_2\cos\theta_2>0$: contradiction.

If $\theta_1+\theta_2=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ then each angle exceeds $\frac\pi2$ (as each is below $\pi$), so both cosines are negative and $\mathrm{Re}(z_1+z_2)<0$: contradiction. So A is impossible; D is the mirror image.
Opposite signs are realised by $z_1=1+i,\ z_2=-1-i$: $z_1z_2=-2i$ and $z_1+z_2=0$. So B and C are possible: option (A).

useful_results: $\mathrm{Re}(z_1z_2)=x_1x_2-y_1y_2$: a product is purely imaginary exactly when $\arg z_1+\arg z_2\equiv\frac\pi2\pmod\pi$.
$\mathrm{Re}(z_1+z_2)=0$ means $x_2=-x_1$ (the numbers are mirror images in the imaginary axis, up to height); then $y_1y_2=-x_1^2\le0$.
Quick test of such 'possible?' options: use $z_2=-z_1$ (sum $0$) - the product is $-z_1^2$, purely imaginary when $z_1$ lies on $y=\pm x$.

concepts: Locus of $z+\frac1z$ on a circle (ellipse)
Intersection of a circle and an ellipse
questions.question: For all $z\in\mathbb{C}$ on the curve $C_1:|z|=4$, let the locus of the point $z+\frac1z$ be the curve $C_2$. Then:
options: the curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ intersect at $4$ points
the curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ intersect at $2$ points
questions.answer: (A) the curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ intersect at $4$ points
questions.key_idea: On $|z|=4$ the point $z+\frac1z$ traces an ellipse with semi-axes $\frac{17}{4}$ and $\frac{15}{4}$; compare them with the circle's radius $4$.
solution: So $C_2$ is the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{(17/4)^2}+\frac{y^2}{(15/4)^2}=1$, while $C_1$ is the circle $x^2+y^2=16$.
The semi-axis along $x$ is $\frac{17}{4}>4$ (ellipse outside the circle there) and along $y$ is $\frac{15}{4}<4$ (ellipse inside the circle there).
So the curves cross; by symmetry about both axes there is one crossing in each quadrant, giving $4$ points of intersection: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Count the intersections as the solutions $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ of $|w|^2=16$ for the point $w=z+\frac1z$ on $C_2$.
solution: A point of $C_2$ lies on $C_1$ exactly when $|w|^2=16$: $4\cos^2\theta=\frac{31}{16}$, i.e. $\cos^2\theta=\frac{31}{64}$.
$\cos\theta=\pm\frac{\sqrt{31}}{8}$, each with two values of $\theta$ in $[0,2\pi)$: four values of $\theta$.
The map $\theta\mapsto w$ is one-to-one on $[0,2\pi)$, so there are exactly $4$ intersection points, option (A).

useful_results: For $|z|=r$ the map $z\mapsto z+\frac1z$ gives the ellipse with semi-axes $r+\frac1r$ (real direction) and $\left|r-\frac1r\right|$ (imaginary direction), foci at $\pm2$ for every $r>0$, $r\neq1$.
For $r=1$ it degenerates to the segment $[-2,2]$; $z-\frac1z$ gives the confocal ellipse with foci $\pm2i$.
A circle of radius $R$ centred at the centre of an ellipse meets it in $4$ points exactly when $b<R<a$ ($b<4<a$ here: $3.75<4<4.25$).

concepts: Argument of a complex number
questions.question: Let $z=1+i$ and $z_1=\frac{1+i\bar z}{\bar z(1-z)+\frac1z}$. Then $\frac{12}{\pi}\arg(z_1)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Substitute $z=1+i$ and rationalise carefully; the quotient simplifies to $-1+i$.
solution: Multiply numerator and denominator by $-1+3i$ (the conjugate of $-1-3i$): $z_1=\frac{(4+2i)(-1+3i)}{10}=\frac{-4+12i-2i-6}{10}=-1+i$.
$-1+i$ lies in the second quadrant, so $\arg z_1=\frac{3\pi}{4}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $z\bar z=|z|^2=2$ to replace $\bar z$ by $\frac2z$ and simplify the expression before substituting.

useful_results: Replace $\bar z$ by $\frac{|z|^2}{z}$ so that a mixed expression becomes a rational function of $z$ alone.
$\arg\frac{a}{b}=\arg a-\arg b$ (mod $2\pi$): here $\tan^{-1}3+\tan^{-1}2=\frac{3\pi}{4}$ because $\tan(\cdot)=\frac{3+2}{1-6}=-1$ with the angle in $\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right)$.
For $a+ib$ always fix the quadrant by the signs of $a,b$ before quoting $\tan^{-1}\frac ba$.

concepts: Polar form and division of complex numbers
questions.question: The complex number $z=\frac{i-1}{\cos\frac\pi3+i\sin\frac\pi3}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Write numerator and denominator in exponential form and subtract the arguments.

alternate_solutions.idea: Divide algebraically (multiply by the conjugate of the denominator) and match the result with the exact values of $\cos75^\circ$ and $\sin75^\circ$.
solution: These match the real and imaginary parts of $z$, so option (C) holds.

useful_results: Dividing by $e^{i\theta}$ subtracts $\theta$ from the argument and divides moduli: $\frac{r_1e^{i\theta_1}}{r_2e^{i\theta_2}}=\frac{r_1}{r_2}e^{i(\theta_1-\theta_2)}$.
Standard forms: $1+i=\sqrt2e^{i\pi/4}$, $i-1=\sqrt2e^{i3\pi/4}$, $1-i=\sqrt2e^{-i\pi/4}$; $\cos75^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}$, $\sin75^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$.
Options can be pruned by modulus first: $|z|=\sqrt2$ rejects (A), which has modulus $1$.

concepts: Circle in the complex plane (circle of Apollonius)
questions.question: If the centre and radius of the circle $\left|\frac{z-2}{z-3}\right|=2$ are respectively $(\alpha,\beta)$ and $\gamma$, then $3(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Cross-multiply, expand with $z\bar z$ and read the centre and radius from $z\bar z+\bar az+a\bar z+c=0$.
solution: Compare with $z\bar z+\bar az+a\bar z+c=0$: $a=-\frac{10}{3}$ and $c=\frac{32}{3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The ends of the diameter are the internal and external points dividing the segment from $2$ to $3$ in the ratio $2:1$.
solution: These are the ends of a diameter on the real axis: centre $\frac{8/3+4}{2}=\frac{10}{3}$, radius $\frac{4-8/3}{2}=\frac23$.

useful_results: $z\bar z+\bar az+a\bar z+c=0$ is a circle with centre $-a$ and radius $\sqrt{|a|^2-c}$ (real if $|a|^2\ge c$).
For $|z-a|=k|z-b|$ with $a,b$ real the centre and the diameter lie on the real axis, so the diameter-end method (internal and external division) is the quickest.
Sanity check: the ratio $\left|\frac{z-2}{z-3}\right|$ is large near $3$, so the circle must enclose $3$ and exclude $2$: it spans $\frac83<3<4$ on the real axis, as found.

concepts: Modulus of a complex number and locus
Greatest integer function
questions.question: Let $a,b$ be two real numbers such that $ab<0$. If the complex number $\frac{1+ai}{b+i}$ is of unit modulus and $a+ib$ lies on the circle $|z-1|=|2z|$, then a possible value of $\frac{1+[a]}{4b}$, where $[t]$ is the greatest integer function, is:
questions.answer: None of the options (the question was dropped)
questions.key_idea: Unit modulus gives $a^2=b^2$, hence $b=-a$; then find $a$ from the circle and test both roots.
solution: Case $a=\frac{-1-\sqrt7}{6}\approx-0.61$: $[a]=-1$, so $1+[a]=0$ and the value is $0$.
The possible values are $-\frac{1+\sqrt7}{4}$ and $0$; none equals $\frac12,-\frac12,1,-1$. No option matches, so the question was dropped (key: Drop).

alternate_solutions.idea: Read $|z-1|=2|z|$ as an Apollonius circle and intersect it with the line $y=-x$ on which $a+ib$ must lie.
solution: $|z-1|=2|z-0|$: circle with centre $\frac{1-4\cdot0}{1-4}=-\frac13$ and radius $\frac{2\cdot1}{3}=\frac23$, i.e. $\left(x+\frac13\right)^2+y^2=\frac49$.
Substituting $y=-x$: $2x^2+\frac23x+\frac19-\frac49=0$, i.e. $6x^2+2x-1=0$ (the same quadratic, now seen as line $\cap$ circle).
So $a=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt7}{6}$; the values of $\frac{1+[a]}{4b}$ are $-\frac{1+\sqrt7}{4}$ and $0$, matching no option.

useful_results: Estimate surds to settle floors: $2.6<\sqrt7<2.7$, so $\frac{\sqrt7-1}{6}\in(0.26,0.29)$ and $\frac{-1-\sqrt7}{6}\in(-0.62,-0.60)$.
$\left|\frac{u+ia}{v+ib}\right|=1\iff u^2+a^2=v^2+b^2$; with $u=v=1$-type constants this is just $a=\pm b$.
Always test every root of the quadratic: here the two roots give different floors and so different values of the expression.

concepts: Locus of complex numbers (lines and circles)
questions.question: Let $\alpha=8-14i$, $A=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\frac{\alpha z-\bar\alpha\bar z}{z^2-(\bar z)^2-112i}=1\right\}$ and $B=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z+3i|=4\}$. Then $\sum_{z\in A\cap B}(\mathrm{Re}\,z-\mathrm{Im}\,z)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\alpha z-\bar\alpha\bar z=2i\,\mathrm{Im}(\alpha z)$ and $z^2-\bar z^2=4ixy$, so $A$ factorises into two lines.
solution: $z-\bar z=2iy$ and $z+\bar z=2x$, so $z^2-\bar z^2=4ixy$ and the denominator is $i(4xy-112)$.
Both points keep the denominator non-zero ($4xy-112=-160$ and $-112$), so $A\cap B=\{4-3i,\,-7i\}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Move everything to one side: the condition says $\mathrm{Im}(z^2-\alpha z)=56$, and completing the square turns it into $\mathrm{Im}\left[(z-\tfrac\alpha2)^2\right]=0$.
solution: $\alpha z-\bar\alpha\bar z=z^2-\bar z^2-112i\iff(z^2-\alpha z)-\overline{(z^2-\alpha z)}=112i\iff2i\,\mathrm{Im}(z^2-\alpha z)=112i$, i.e. $\mathrm{Im}(z^2-\alpha z)=56$.
A square is real exactly when the number is real or purely imaginary: $z-(4-7i)$ is real ($y=-7$) or purely imaginary ($x=4$).

useful_results: $w-\bar w=2i\,\mathrm{Im}\,w$ and $z^2-\bar z^2=4i\,\mathrm{Re}z\,\mathrm{Im}z$: conditions on $\frac{w-\bar w}{\cdot}$ often reduce to a single $\mathrm{Im}$ equation.
$\mathrm{Im}(w^2)=0\iff w\in\mathbb{R}\cup i\mathbb{R}$: a degenerate hyperbola $2uv=0$, i.e. two perpendicular lines through the centre $w=0$.
Completing the square in $z$ ($z^2-\alpha z=(z-\frac\alpha2)^2-\frac{\alpha^2}{4}$) locates the centre of a conic $xy+px+qy+r=0$ at $(-q,-p)$: here $(4,-7)$.

concepts: Real part of expressions in $z$ and $\bar z$
questions.question: Let $a\neq b$ be two non-zero real numbers. Then the number of elements in the set $X=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}(az^2+bz)=a\ \text{and}\ \mathrm{Re}(bz^2+az)=b\right\}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Each condition is linear in the two real quantities $x^2-y^2$ and $x$; solve the $2\times2$ system and treat $b=-a$ separately.
solution: $\mathrm{Re}(az^2+bz)=a\Rightarrow az^2+bz+a\bar z^2+b\bar z=2a\Rightarrow a(z^2+\bar z^2)+b(z+\bar z)=2a$ ... (1).
With $z+\bar z=0$: $z^2+\bar z^2=(z+\bar z)^2-2z\bar z=-2|z|^2$, so $-2|z|^2=2$, i.e. $|z|^2=-1$: impossible. Hence $X=\emptyset$ when $a\neq\pm b$.
If $b=-a$ (allowed, since only $a\neq b$ is assumed), (1) and (2) both reduce to $\mathrm{Re}(z^2-z)=1$, i.e. $x^2-y^2-x=1$.
For every real $y$ this gives two values of $x$, so $X$ is then an infinite set. The key (D) $0$ therefore holds for $a\neq\pm b$ only.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's own last lines show that for $a=-b$ there are infinitely many solutions (the hyperbola $x^2-y^2-x=1$), yet the key is $0$. The answer $0$ is correct only for $a\neq\pm b$ (generic $a,b$). Kept the key (D) and made the restriction explicit. The question as printed does not exclude $a=-b$, so it is not fully well posed.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $u=x^2-y^2=\mathrm{Re}(z^2)$ and $x=\mathrm{Re}(z)$: the two conditions become a linear system in $(u,x)$.
solution: Cramer's rule: $u=\frac{a\cdot a-b\cdot b}{a^2-b^2}=1$ and $x=\frac{a\cdot b-b\cdot a}{a^2-b^2}=0$.
$x=0$ and $x^2-y^2=1$ give $-y^2=1$, impossible for real $y$, so $X=\emptyset$: option (D).
When $b=-a$ the determinant vanishes and both equations coincide ($u-x=1$), giving the hyperbola $x^2-y^2-x=1$ with infinitely many points.

useful_results: $\mathrm{Re}(z)=x$ and $\mathrm{Re}(z^2)=x^2-y^2$: conditions on real parts of several polynomials in $z$ are linear in $(1,\,x,\,x^2-y^2,\,\dots)$, so use Cramer's rule.
A zero determinant ($b=\pm a$ here) signals a special case that must be examined separately; it can change a finite or empty answer into a one-dimensional family.
Impossibility check: $\mathrm{Re}(z^2)=x^2-y^2\ge-y^2$, so $x=0$ forces $\mathrm{Re}(z^2)\le0$, which cannot equal $1$.

concepts: Modulus and equality of complex numbers
Quadratic equation from sum and product of roots
questions.question: If for $z=\alpha+i\beta$, $|z+2|=z+4(1+i)$, then $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ are the roots of the equation:
questions.key_idea: A modulus is real, so the imaginary part of $z+4(1+i)$ must vanish; that gives $\beta$ at once.
solution: Squaring: $\alpha^2+4\alpha+4+16=\alpha^2+8\alpha+16$, so $4\alpha=4$ and $\alpha=1$ (and $\alpha+4=5>0$, so no extraneous root).
The equation with these roots is $x^2-(-3-4)x+(-3)(-4)=0$, i.e. $x^2+7x+12=0$: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Call the common real value $t=|z+2|$; then $z=t-4-4i$ immediately and a single equation in $t$ remains.
solution: The roots are $\alpha+\beta=-3$ and $\alpha\beta=-4$, so $x^2+7x+12=0$: option (A).

useful_results: If a real number or a modulus equals a complex expression, that expression must be real (and non-negative for a modulus): equate imaginary parts first.
Introduce the common real value as a new unknown ($t=|z+2|$) to write $z$ explicitly in one step.
Squaring can create extraneous roots: always re-check the sign condition (here $\alpha+4=5>0$). Roots $r_1,r_2$ give $x^2-(r_1+r_2)x+r_1r_2=0$.

concepts: Purely imaginary complex number
Trigonometric equations
questions.question: Let $A=\left\{\theta\in(0,2\pi):\frac{1+2i\sin\theta}{1-i\sin\theta}\ \text{is purely imaginary}\right\}$. Then the sum of the elements in $A$ is:
questions.key_idea: Rationalise the denominator; the real part is $\frac{1-2\sin^2\theta}{1+\sin^2\theta}$ and must be zero.
solution: Purely imaginary means real part $=0$ (and imaginary part $\ne0$): $\frac{1-2\sin^2\theta}{1+\sin^2\theta}=0$.
So $\sin^2\theta=\frac12$; then $\sin\theta=\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}\ne0$, so the imaginary part is non-zero.

alternate_solutions.idea: The condition depends only on $\sin^2\theta$, so solutions pair up as $\theta\leftrightarrow2\pi-\theta$; count the solutions and add the pairs.
solution: $2\theta\in(0,4\pi)$ and $\cos2\theta=0$ gives $2\theta=\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{5\pi}{2},\frac{7\pi}{2}$: exactly four values of $\theta$.
$\cos2\theta$ is unchanged under $\theta\mapsto2\pi-\theta$, and this map has no fixed point in the solution set, so the four solutions form two pairs, each pair summing to $2\pi$.

useful_results: $\frac{1+ia}{1-ib}=\frac{(1+ia)(1+ib)}{1+b^2}$ has real part $\frac{1-ab}{1+b^2}$ and imaginary part $\frac{a+b}{1+b^2}$; 'purely imaginary' also needs $a+b\ne0$.

If a trigonometric condition depends on $\sin^2\theta$ or $\cos2\theta$ only, its roots in $(0,2\pi)$ come in pairs $\theta,\ 2\pi-\theta$ (and $\theta,\ \pi\mp\theta$): the sum of all roots of $\sin^2\theta=c$ ($0<c<1$) is $4\pi$.
For $\cos2\theta=0$ in $(0,2\pi)$ the four roots are $\frac\pi4+\frac{k\pi}{2}$, $k=0,1,2,3$, in arithmetic progression: sum $=4\cdot\frac{\pi/4+7\pi/4}{2}=4\pi$.

concepts: Purely imaginary complex number
questions.question: Let the complex number $z=x+iy$ be such that $\frac{2z-3i}{2z+i}$ is purely imaginary. If $x+y^2=0$, then $y^4+y^2-y$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Purely imaginary means real part $0$; this gives $4x^2+4y^2-4y-3=0$, and $x=-y^2$ finishes it.
solution: $\frac{2z-3i}{2z+i}=\frac{2x+i(2y-3)}{2x+i(2y+1)}$ is purely imaginary, so its real part is $0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\frac{2z-3i}{2z+i}=\frac{z-\frac{3i}{2}}{z+\frac i2}$ is purely imaginary exactly when $z$ lies on the circle with diameter joining $\frac{3i}{2}$ and $-\frac i2$ (a right angle at $z$).
solution: $\frac{z-\frac{3i}{2}}{z+\frac i2}$ purely imaginary means $\arg=\pm\frac\pi2$: the segment from $-\frac i2$ to $\frac{3i}{2}$ subtends a right angle at $z$.
So $z$ lies on the circle with diameter $\left\{-\frac i2,\frac{3i}{2}\right\}$: centre $\frac i2$, radius $1$: $x^2+\left(y-\frac12\right)^2=1$, i.e. $x^2+y^2-y-\frac34=0$.

useful_results: $\frac{z-a}{z-b}$ is purely imaginary $\iff z$ is on the circle with diameter $ab$ ($z\ne a,b$); real $\iff z$ is on line $ab$; of modulus $1\iff z$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $ab$.
General: $\frac{z-a}{z-b}$ has argument $\pm\frac\pi4$ on an arc through $a,b$ (the angle subtended by $ab$).
$\mathrm{Re}\frac{p+iq}{r+is}=\frac{pr+qs}{r^2+s^2}$ - real part is the dot product of the two vectors.

concepts: Real-valued expression in $z$ and its locus
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{z=x+iy:\frac{2z-3i}{4z+2i}\ \text{is a real number}\right\}$. Then which of the following is NOT correct:
questions.key_idea: The ratio is real only on the line $x=0$, with the single point $z=-\frac i2$ (where the denominator vanishes) removed.
solution: Multiply by the conjugate $4x-(4y+2)i$; the imaginary part of the numerator is $-2x(4y+2)+(2y-3)4x=-16x$.

The denominator must be non-zero: $4z+2i
eq0$, i.e. $z
e- rac i2$, so $y
e- rac12$.
(A) $y+x^2+y^2=\left(y+\frac12\right)^2-\frac14\neq-\frac14$ is true for $x=0$; (B) is true; (D) is true; (C) names the excluded point, so it is NOT correct: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Divide first: $\frac{2z-3i}{2z+i}=1-\frac{4i}{2z+i}$, so the ratio is real iff $\frac{4i}{2z+i}$ is real, iff $2z+i$ is purely imaginary.
solution: This is real iff $\frac{4i}{2z+i}$ is real, iff $\frac{2z+i}{i}$ is real, iff $2z+i\in i\mathbb{R}$, i.e. $\mathrm{Re}(2z)=0$: $x=0$.
The denominator $2z+i=2iy+i$ vanishes only at $y=-\frac12$, which is excluded. So $S=\{(0,y):y\ne-\frac12\}$ and (C) is the incorrect statement.

useful_results: $\frac{az+b}{cz+d}=\frac ac+\frac{bc-ad}{c(cz+d)}$: the real/imaginary behaviour is that of $\frac{bc-ad}{cz+d}$ alone.
$\frac{k}{w}$ is real iff $w$ is a real multiple of $k$: here $\frac{4i}{2z+i}$ real iff $2z+i\in i\mathbb{R}$, a vertical line - this is the line through the pole in the direction of $k$.
'Is real' problems exclude the pole of the expression: always remove the point where the denominator is zero.

concepts: Rotation and principal argument of a complex number
questions.question: Let $w_1$ be the point obtained by the rotation of $z_1=5+4i$ about the origin through a right angle in the anticlockwise direction, and $w_2$ be the point obtained by the rotation of $z_2=3+5i$ about the origin through a right angle in the clockwise direction. Then the principal argument of $w_1-w_2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: An anticlockwise right-angle rotation multiplies by $i$, a clockwise one by $-i$.
solution: $-9+8i$ is in the second quadrant, so the principal argument is $\pi-\tan^{-1}\frac89$: option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: $w_1-w_2=iz_1-(-iz_2)=i(z_1+z_2)$, so the answer is $\frac\pi2+\arg(z_1+z_2)$.

useful_results: Rotation about the origin through $\theta$ anticlockwise: $z\mapsto e^{i\theta}z$; $90^\circ$: $\times i$; $-90^\circ$: $\times(-i)$; $180^\circ$: $\times(-1)$.
$\arg(iu)=\arg u+\frac\pi2$ and $\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}\frac1x=\frac\pi2$ for $x>0$: this converts between forms like $\frac\pi2+\tan^{-1}\frac98$ and $\pi-\tan^{-1}\frac89$.
Quadrant check eliminates options: $-9+8i$ is in the second quadrant, so the principal argument lies in $\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right)$ - options (A) and (C) are negative angles.

concepts: Real and imaginary parts of complex numbers
questions.question:
For $a\in\mathbb{C}$, let $A=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}(a+\bar z)>\mathrm{Im}(\bar a+z)\}$ and $B=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}(a+\bar z)<\mathrm{Im}(\bar a+z)\}$. Then among the two statements:
(S1): If $\mathrm{Re}(a),\mathrm{Im}(a)>0$, then the set $A$ contains all the real numbers.
(S2): If $\mathrm{Re}(a),\mathrm{Im}(a)<0$, then the set $B$ contains all the real numbers.
questions.key_idea: For real $z=x$ each inequality becomes a linear inequality in $x$, which has only a half-line of solutions.
solution: $A$: $x_1+x>-y_1+y$. For real $z$ ($y=0$) this is $x>-(x_1+y_1)$, which fails for every $x\le-(x_1+y_1)$.
Counter-example for (S1): $a=2+10i$ (both parts positive), $z=-12$: $-10>-10$ is false. So (S1) is false.
$B$: $x_1+x<-y_1+y$. For real $z$ this is $x<-(x_1+y_1)$, which fails for large positive $x$.
Counter-example for (S2): $a=-2-10i$ (both parts negative), $z=12$: $10<10$ is false. So (S2) is false.
useful_results: $\mathrm{Re}(\bar w)=\mathrm{Re}\,w$ and $\mathrm{Im}(\bar w)=-\mathrm{Im}\,w$; for $z=x$ real, $\mathrm{Re}(a+\bar z)-\mathrm{Im}(\bar a+z)=x+(x_1+y_1)$.
A non-constant linear inequality in a real variable always has a half-line solution set, so a claim that it holds for 'all real $x$' can only be true if the $x$-coefficient is zero.
The signs of $\mathrm{Re}\,a$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,a$ only shift the threshold $-(x_1+y_1)$; they never make the inequality hold for all real $x$.

concepts: Distance and collinearity in the complex plane
questions.question: Let $C$ be the circle in the complex plane with centre $z_0=\frac12(1+3i)$ and radius $r=1$. Let $z_1=1+i$ and the complex number $z_2$ be outside the circle $C$ such that $|z_1-z_0||z_2-z_0|=1$. If $z_0,z_1$ and $z_2$ are collinear, then the smaller value of $|z_2|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The product condition fixes $|z_2-z_0|=\sqrt2$; collinearity gives two points on the line $z_0z_1$, one on each side of $z_0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Inversion in the circle: collinear points with $|z_1-z_0||z_2-z_0|=r^2$ satisfy $z_2-z_0=\pm\frac{z_1-z_0}{|z_1-z_0|^2}$.
solution: $z_2-z_0$ is a real multiple of $z_1-z_0$ with modulus $\frac1{|z_1-z_0|}$, so $z_2-z_0=\pm\frac{z_1-z_0}{|z_1-z_0|^2}$.

useful_results: Inversion in the circle $|z-c|=r$: $z\mapsto c+\frac{r^2}{\overline{z-c}}$; it keeps the point on the ray through $c$ and gives $|z-c||z'-c|=r^2$. The point on the opposite ray is its reflection in $c$: both satisfy the product condition.
If a point is inside the circle its inverse is outside and vice versa; points on the circle are fixed.
A problem with a product of distances equal to a constant and collinearity usually has two answers (one per side of the centre) - check both and choose as asked.

concepts: Complex roots of a quadratic and De Moivre's theorem
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2-\sqrt2x+2=0$. Then $\alpha^{14}+\beta^{14}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The roots are conjugates of modulus $\sqrt2$ and argument $\pm\frac\pi3$, so $\alpha^{14}+\beta^{14}=2\cdot2^7\cos\frac{14\pi}{3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Square once: $\alpha^2,\beta^2$ are the roots of $t^2+2t+4=0$, i.e. $2\omega$ and $2\omega^2$, so the 7th power uses $\omega^3=1$.

useful_results: Roots of $x^2-px+q=0$ with $p^2<4q$: modulus $\sqrt q$ and argument $\pm\cos^{-1}\frac{p}{2\sqrt q}$ (here $\cos^{-1}\frac12=\frac\pi3$), so $\alpha^n+\beta^n=2q^{n/2}\cos(n\theta)$.
Squaring a quadratic's roots changes $(p,q)$ to $(p^2-2q,\,q^2)$; a few squarings often land on $\pm1\pm\sqrt3i$-type roots, i.e. cube roots of unity times a constant.
Instance: $2\cdot2^7\cos\frac{14\pi}{3}=256\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-128$.

concepts: Equations in $z$ and $\bar z$
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\bar z=i\left(z^2+\mathrm{Re}(\bar z)\right)\right\}$. Then $\sum_{z\in S}|z|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Split the equation into real and imaginary parts: the real part factorises as $x(2y+1)=0$, giving two cases.
solution: Case $y=-\frac12$: (ii) gives $\frac12=x^2-\frac14+x$, i.e. $x^2+x-\frac34=0$, $(2x-1)(2x+3)=0$, so $x=\frac12$ or $-\frac32$: $z=\frac12-\frac i2$ or $-\frac32-\frac i2$.
useful_results: For equations mixing $z$, $\bar z$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,z$, put $z=x+iy$ and split into two real equations; look for a factorised one to branch.
Always check the case split is exhaustive and verify each solution by substitution, e.g. $z=i$: $\bar z=-i$ and $i(i^2+0)=-i$ ✓.
$\sum|z|^2=\sum(x^2+y^2)$ is not obtainable by Vieta here (the system is not a polynomial in $z$ alone), so list the solutions.

concepts: Range of a real part of a rational expression in $z$
questions.question: If the set $\left\{\mathrm{Re}\left(\frac{z-\bar z+z\bar z}{2-3z+5\bar z}\right):z\in\mathbb{C},\ \mathrm{Re}(z)=3\right\}$ is equal to the interval $(\alpha,\beta]$, then $24(\beta-\alpha)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: On $\mathrm{Re}\,z=3$ the real part becomes $\frac18\left(\frac{10}{1+y^2}-1\right)$, whose range is read off from $1+y^2\ge1$.
solution: Let $z=3+iy$, $\bar z=3-iy$: $z-\bar z=2iy$ and $z\bar z=9+y^2$, so the numerator is $9+y^2+2iy$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $y=\tan\varphi$ so that $\frac1{1+y^2}=\cos^2\varphi$ and the range follows from $\cos2\varphi$.
solution: $2\varphi\in(-\pi,\pi)$, so $\cos2\varphi\in(-1,1]$ ($-1$ is not attained, $1$ is attained at $\varphi=0$).

useful_results: $\mathrm{Re}\frac{p+iq}{r(1-iy)}=\frac{p+qy}{r(1+y^2)}$-type expressions: multiply by $(1+iy)$ and use $1+y^2$ as the denominator; the range of $\frac{c-y^2}{1+y^2}=\frac{c+1}{1+y^2}-1$ is $(-1,c]$ for $c>-1$.
An endpoint is attained only if the underlying parameter value exists: $y=0$ gives $\frac98$, but $-\frac18$ needs $y\to\infty$, so it is excluded (note $(\alpha,\beta]$).
Substituting $y=\tan\varphi$ turns $\frac{1}{1+y^2}$ into $\cos^2\varphi$ and rational functions of $y$ into trigonometric ranges.

concepts: Circle in the complex plane
Apollonius theorem (sum of squared distances)
questions.question: For $\alpha,\beta,z\in\mathbb{C}$ and $\lambda>1$, if $\sqrt{\lambda-1}$ is the radius of the circle $|z-\alpha|^2+|z-\beta|^2=2\lambda$, then $|\alpha-\beta|$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: With $c=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$: $|z-\alpha|^2+|z-\beta|^2=2|z-c|^2+\frac12|\alpha-\beta|^2$, so the radius is read off directly.
solution: Adding the squares of the moduli, the cross terms cancel: $|z-\alpha|^2+|z-\beta|^2=2|z-c|^2+\frac12|\alpha-\beta|^2$.
This is a circle with centre $c$ and $(\text{radius})^2=\lambda-\frac14|\alpha-\beta|^2$.
The radius is given as $\sqrt{\lambda-1}$: $\lambda-\frac14|\alpha-\beta|^2=\lambda-1$, so $|\alpha-\beta|^2=4$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF applies the diameter-circle identity $|z-z_1|^2+|z-z_2|^2=|z_1-z_2|^2$, which holds only when $2\lambda=|\alpha-\beta|^2$; that assumption is not given. Its answer 2 is right, but the working is not justified (the answer is independent of $\lambda$). Replaced by the general identity.

alternate_solutions.idea: Choose coordinates in which $\alpha=-d$ and $\beta=d$ are real and symmetric about the origin; then the circle's radius is immediate.
solution: Translate and rotate so that the midpoint of $\alpha,\beta$ is $0$ and $\alpha=-d,\ \beta=d$ with $d=\frac{|\alpha-\beta|}{2}$ (distances and radii do not change).

useful_results: Apollonius / parallelogram identity: $|z-a|^2+|z-b|^2=2\left|z-\frac{a+b}{2}\right|^2+\frac12|a-b|^2$.
So $|z-a|^2+|z-b|^2=k$ is a circle centred at the midpoint of $ab$ with radius$^2=\frac k2-\frac{|a-b|^2}{4}$ (real only if $k\ge\frac{|a-b|^2}{2}$); $k=|a-b|^2$ gives the circle on $ab$ as diameter.
Instance: $k=2\lambda$ gives $r^2=\lambda-\frac{|\alpha-\beta|^2}{4}$; setting $r^2=\lambda-1$ gives $|\alpha-\beta|=2$ for every $\lambda>1$.

concepts: Real-valued rational expression in $z$
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}-\{i,2i\}:\frac{z^2+8iz-15}{z^2-3iz-2}\in\mathbb{R}\right\}$. If $\alpha-\frac{13}{11}i\in S$, $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}-\{0\}$, then $242\alpha^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Subtract the denominator from the numerator: the fraction is $1+\frac{11iz-13}{z^2-3iz-2}$, and at $z=\alpha-\frac{13}{11}i$ the top is $11i\alpha$, purely imaginary.
solution: $z^2-3iz-2=(z-i)(z-2i)$, so $z\ne i,2i$ keeps the denominator non-zero.
Put $z=\alpha-\frac{13}{11}i$: $11iz=11i\alpha+13$, so $11iz-13=11i\alpha$ - purely imaginary and non-zero ($\alpha\neq0$).
For the fraction to be real, $\frac{11i\alpha}{z^2-3iz-2}$ must be real, so $z^2-3iz-2$ must be purely imaginary: its real part is $0$.
useful_results: To test whether $\frac{N}{D}$ is real, split $\frac ND=1+\frac{N-D}{D}$ when $N-D$ is simple: here it is $11iz-13$, a linear expression that becomes purely imaginary on the given line.
A real quotient of a purely imaginary non-zero number needs the denominator to be purely imaginary (real part $0$): this gives the rectangular hyperbola $x^2-\left(y-\frac32\right)^2=-\frac14$.
$z^2-3iz-2=(z-i)(z-2i)$ and $z^2+8iz-15=(z+3i)(z+5i)$: always factor first to see the excluded points.

concepts: Circle and line from real and imaginary parts of $w$
Chord length of a circle
questions.question: Let $w=z\bar z+k_1z+k_2iz+\lambda(1+i)$, $k_1,k_2\in\mathbb{R}$. Let $\mathrm{Re}(w)=0$ be the circle $C$ of radius $1$ in the first quadrant touching the line $y=1$ and the $y$-axis. If the curve $\mathrm{Im}(w)=0$ intersects $C$ at $A$ and $B$, then $30(AB)^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\mathrm{Re}(w)=0$ is the circle $x^2+y^2+k_1x-k_2y+\lambda=0$ and $\mathrm{Im}(w)=0$ is the line $k_2x+k_1y+\lambda=0$; the chord is $2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$.
solution: Radius $1$ touching the $y$-axis (centre at $x=1$) and the line $y=1$ while lying in the first quadrant: the centre is $(1,2)$ (centre $(1,0)$ would put part of the circle below the $x$-axis).
Distance of the centre $(1,2)$ from this line: $d=\frac{|2-2+2|}{\sqrt5}=\frac{2}{\sqrt5}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops after writing the line $2x-y+2=0$; it does not explain why the centre is $(1,2)$ rather than $(1,0)$, does not compute the chord $AB$ and never reaches $30(AB)^2=24$. Added the missing steps; the answer 24 agrees with the key.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $A$ and $B$ explicitly by substituting the line into the circle.
solution: $A=(0,2)$ (the point where the circle touches the $y$-axis) and $B=\left(\frac25,\frac{14}{5}\right)$.

useful_results: For $w=z\bar z+az+b\bar z+c$-type expressions: $\mathrm{Re}\,w=0$ is a circle and $\mathrm{Im}\,w=0$ is a line; their intersection is found as a chord: $AB=2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$.
Here $\mathrm{Re}(k_2iz)=-k_2y$ and $\mathrm{Im}(k_2iz)=k_2x$ - multiplying by $i$ swaps the roles of $x$ and $y$.

A circle of radius $r$ in the first quadrant touching both axes has centre $(r,r)$; touching $x=0$ and $y=1$ with radius $1$ gives centre $(1,2)$ (above $y=1$), the other choice $(1,0)$ leaves the quadrant.

concepts: Perpendicular bisector loci in the complex plane
questions.question: If $S=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-i|=|z+i|=|z-1|\}$, then $n(S)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Equal distances from two points give a perpendicular bisector; two such lines meet in one point.
solution: $|z-i|=|z+i|$: $z$ is equidistant from $i=(0,1)$ and $-i=(0,-1)$, so it lies on their perpendicular bisector, the real axis $y=0$.
$|z-i|=|z-1|$: $z$ is equidistant from $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector $y=x$.
The two lines $y=0$ and $y=x$ meet only at $(0,0)$, so $z=0$ is the only candidate.
questions.correction_note: The PDF gives only a hand-drawn sketch of three lines with no working. Wrote the solution (two perpendicular bisectors meeting at the origin, plus the check).

alternate_solutions.idea: A point equidistant from three non-collinear points is their circumcentre, which exists and is unique.
solution: These three points are not collinear (two are on the imaginary axis, $1$ is off it).
They all lie on the unit circle $|z|=1$, so the circumcentre is $0$ and it is the only such point.

useful_results: Points equidistant from three non-collinear points: exactly one (the circumcentre); from three collinear points: none unless the points coincide; from two points: the perpendicular bisector.
If three given points visibly lie on $|z-c|=R$, then $c$ is the circumcentre - spot it from the moduli (here $|i|=|-i|=|1|=1$).
The same reading works in the complex plane for $|z-a|=|z-b|=|z-c'|$ with any three distinct non-collinear $a,b,c'$.

concepts: Modulus and equality of complex numbers
questions.question: If $z=\frac12-2i$ is such that $|z+1|=\alpha z+\beta(1+i)$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$, then $\alpha+\beta$ is:
questions.key_idea: A modulus is real, so the imaginary part of $\alpha z+\beta(1+i)$ must vanish.
solution: The left side is real, so the imaginary part is zero: $-2\alpha+\beta=0$, i.e. $\beta=2\alpha$.
useful_results: If a modulus (a non-negative real) equals a complex expression, equate imaginary parts to $0$ first: it often gives a linear relation between the unknowns.
$|a+ib|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$: $\left|\frac32-2i\right|=\frac52$ comes from the $3,4,5$ triangle with sides $\frac32,2,\frac52$ scaled by $\frac12$.
Real unknowns $\alpha,\beta$ multiplying complex numbers give two real equations (real and imaginary parts), a $2\times2$ linear system.

concepts: Modulus and amplitude of a complex number
Trigonometric ratios of angles in the second quadrant
questions.question: Let $r$ and $\theta$ respectively be the modulus and amplitude of the complex number $z=2-i\left(2\tan\frac{5\pi}{8}\right)$. Then $(r,\theta)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\tan\frac{5\pi}{8}$ is negative, so the imaginary part is positive: $z=2+2\tan\frac{3\pi}{8}\,i$ lies in the first quadrant.
solution: $z=2-i\left(-2\tan\frac{3\pi}{8}\right)=2+2\tan\frac{3\pi}{8}\,i$: real part $2>0$, imaginary part $>0$, first quadrant.
$\tan\theta=\frac{2\tan(3\pi/8)}{2}=\tan\frac{3\pi}{8}$ and $\theta$ is in the first quadrant, so $\theta=\frac{3\pi}{8}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Factor $z=2\sec\varphi\,e^{-i\varphi}$ with $\varphi=\frac{5\pi}{8}$ and absorb the negative sign of $\sec\varphi$ as a rotation by $\pi$.

useful_results: $1+i\tan\varphi=\sec\varphi\,e^{i\varphi}$ for $\varphi\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$; for other $\varphi$ first reduce with $\tan(\pi-\varphi)=-\tan\varphi$ so that the modulus factor $\sec$ is positive.
Modulus is never negative: if the factored form has a negative real multiplier, rotate the argument by $\pi$.
Amplitude must be the principal value: check the quadrant from the signs of the real and imaginary parts (here both positive, so $\theta\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$).

concepts: Modulus properties in equations with $z$ and $\bar z$
questions.question: If $z=x+iy$, $xy\neq0$, satisfies the equation $z^2+i\bar z=0$, then $|z^2|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Take moduli of $z^2=-i\bar z$: $|z|^2=|z|$, and $z\neq0$ forces $|z|=1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Work in Cartesian form: split $z^2+i\bar z=0$ into real and imaginary parts and solve for $x,y$.

useful_results: Equations of the form $z^m=c\,\bar z^{\,n}$: take moduli to get $|z|^{m-n}=|c|$, so $|z|$ is found at once (here $|z|^{2-1}=1$).
Multiplying $z^2=-i\bar z$ by $z$ gives $z^3=-i|z|^2=-i$, so the non-zero solutions are the cube roots of $-i$: $i,\ e^{-i\pi/6},\ e^{i7\pi/6}$ ($z=i$ is excluded by $xy\neq0$).
$|z^2|=|z|^2$ always; $z\bar z=|z|^2$ links the conjugate to the modulus.

concepts: Cube roots of unity
Roots of polynomial equations
questions.question: If $z$ is a complex number, then the number of common roots of the equations $z^{1985}+z^{100}+1=0$ and $z^3+2z^2+2z+1=0$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $z^3+2z^2+2z+1=(z+1)(z^2+z+1)$; test the three roots $-1,\omega,\omega^2$ in the first equation using $\omega^3=1$.
solution: $z=-1$: $(-1)^{1985}+(-1)^{100}+1=-1+1+1=1\neq0$, so $-1$ is not a root of the first equation.
Exactly two common roots, $\omega$ and $\omega^2$: option (D).
questions.correction_note: The PDF says '$\omega,\omega^2$ are the roots of the first equation' without verifying it, and never factors the cubic or tests its third root $-1$ (needed to rule out a third common root). Added both checks; the answer $2$ is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reduce the first polynomial modulo $z^2+z+1$ (where $z^3\equiv1$) and modulo $z+1$; the common roots are the roots of the gcd.
solution: Modulo $z^2+z+1$ we have $z^3\equiv1$, so $z^{1985}\equiv z^{2}$ and $z^{100}\equiv z$: the first polynomial $\equiv z^2+z+1\equiv0$. Hence $z^2+z+1$ divides it.
At $z=-1$ the first polynomial equals $1\neq0$, so $z+1$ does not divide it.
The gcd is $z^2+z+1$, whose two roots are the common roots: the number is $2$ (D).

useful_results: For a primitive cube root of unity, $\omega^a+\omega^b+1=0$ exactly when $\{a\bmod3,\ b\bmod3\}=\{1,2\}$; here $1985\equiv2$ and $100\equiv1$.
$z^2+z+1$ divides $z^a+z^b+1$ iff $\{a,b\}\equiv\{1,2\}\pmod3$ (this one fact answers many 'common roots' questions).
Common roots of two polynomials = roots of their gcd; factor the smaller polynomial and test each of its roots.

concepts: Symmetric functions of two complex numbers
questions.question: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be two complex numbers such that $z_1+z_2=5$ and $z_1^3+z_2^3=20+15i$. Then $\left|z_1^4+z_2^4\right|$ equals:
questions.key_idea: Use $z_1^3+z_2^3=(z_1+z_2)^3-3z_1z_2(z_1+z_2)$ to find $z_1z_2$, then build the fourth power sum from $z_1+z_2$ and $z_1z_2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $z_1,z_2$ themselves: they are the roots of $t^2-5t+(7-i)=0$ and the discriminant is a perfect square.
solution: $z_1+z_2=5$ and $z_1z_2=7-i$ (found as before), so $z_{1,2}$ are roots of $t^2-5t+7-i=0$.

useful_results: Newton's identities hold for complex numbers: $p_n=e_1p_{n-1}-e_2p_{n-2}$ with $e_1=z_1+z_2$, $e_2=z_1z_2$. Here $p_1=5$, $p_2=11+2i$, $p_3=20+15i$, $p_4=21+72i$.
The discriminant $e_1^2-4e_2=-3+4i=(1+2i)^2$ is a perfect square because $z_1,z_2$ are Gaussian integers; $\sqrt{a+bi}$ can be found by solving $(p+qi)^2=a+bi$.

concepts: Intersection of a line and a circle in the complex plane
Maximum and minimum modulus
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-1|=1\ \text{and}\ (\sqrt2-1)(z+\bar z)-i(z-\bar z)=2\sqrt2\right\}$. Let $z_1,z_2\in S$ be such that $|z_1|=\max_{z\in S}|z|$ and $|z_2|=\min_{z\in S}|z|$. Then $\left|\sqrt2z_1-z_2\right|^2$ equals:
questions.key_idea: $S$ is the intersection of a circle and a line, i.e. two points; find them and compare their moduli.
solution: $x=1$ is a root; the product of the roots is $\frac{2}{4-2\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{2-\sqrt2}$, so the other root is $x=\frac{1}{2-\sqrt2}=\frac{2+\sqrt2}{2}$.
$\sqrt2z_1=(\sqrt2+1)+i$ (the PDF writes the real part as $\frac{1}{\sqrt2-1}=\sqrt2+1$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise the circle as $z=1+e^{i\varphi}$; the line becomes $(\sqrt2-1)\cos\varphi+\sin\varphi=1$ with two obvious solutions.
solution: $\varphi=\frac\pi2$ works ($0+1=1$) and $\varphi=\frac\pi4$ works ($\frac{\sqrt2-1}{\sqrt2}+\frac1{\sqrt2}=1$). A line meets a circle in at most two points, so these are all of $S$.
$z_1=1+e^{i\pi/4}$ and $z_2=1+i$. Then $\sqrt2z_1=\sqrt2+\sqrt2e^{i\pi/4}=\sqrt2+(1+i)$, so $\sqrt2z_1-z_2=\sqrt2$ and the square of the modulus is $2$: option (B).

useful_results: A circle $|z-c|=r$ is parametrised as $z=c+re^{i\varphi}$; a line $px+qy=k$ then becomes $p\cos\varphi+q\sin\varphi=k'$, a standard trigonometric equation with at most two solutions in $[0,2\pi)$.
For a circle through the origin ($|c|=r$) the modulus is simple: $|1+e^{i\varphi}|=2\left|\cos\frac\varphi2\right|$.
When a quadratic from line $\cap$ circle has a visible root (here $x=1$), get the other root from the product (or sum) of roots instead of the quadratic formula.

concepts: Minimum distance from a point to a region in the complex plane
questions.question: If $z$ is a complex number such that $|z|\geq1$, then the minimum value of $\left|z+\frac12(3+4i)\right|$ is:
questions.answer: No option is correct (Bonus): the minimum is $0$
questions.key_idea: The fixed point $-\frac12(3+4i)$ already lies in the region $|z|\ge1$, so the distance can be $0$.
solution: $|Q|=\frac12\sqrt{9+16}=\frac52>1$, so $Q$ itself lies in the allowed region $|z|\ge1$.
Taking $z=Q$ gives $PQ=0$, and a modulus cannot be negative, so the minimum value is $0$ (attained when $P$ coincides with $Q$).
$0$ is not among $3,\ \frac52,\ 2,\ \frac32$: the question has no correct option and was given as a Bonus. (For the region $|z|\le1$ the minimum would be $\frac52-1=\frac32$.)
useful_results: Min/max of $|z-a|$ over a region: if $a$ lies in the region the minimum is $0$; for the disc $|z|\le r$ with $|a|>r$: min $=|a|-r$, max $=|a|+r$; for the exterior $|z|\ge r$ with $|a|<r$: min $=r-|a|$.
First locate the fixed point $a$ relative to the region: that decides everything. Here $|a|=\frac52>1$ and the region is the exterior of the unit circle, so $a$ is inside the region.
If no option matches your computed answer, re-read the question for a reversed inequality before choosing - but report what is actually computed.

concepts: Cube roots of unity
Binomial expansion
questions.question: If $\alpha$ satisfies the equation $x^2+x+1=0$ and $(1+\alpha)^7=A+B\alpha+C\alpha^2$, $A,B,C\geq0$, then $5(3A-2B-C)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\alpha$ is a primitive cube root of unity, so expand $(1+\alpha)^7$ and reduce the powers with $\alpha^3=1$.
solution: $\alpha^2+\alpha+1=0$, so $\alpha$ is a non-real cube root of unity: $\alpha^3=1$ (take $\alpha=\omega$).
Constant term: $1+35+7=43$; coefficient of $\alpha$: $7+35+1=43$; coefficient of $\alpha^2$: $21+21=42$.
questions.correction_note: One line of the PDF's expansion has a typo: it writes $24\alpha^5$ instead of $\binom75=21$ (the next line uses $21$ correctly). Corrected the coefficient; the final values $A=43,B=43,C=42$ and the answer $5$ are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $1+\alpha=-\alpha^2$ to shrink the power first, then $1+\alpha+\alpha^2=0$ to express the result in the required form.

useful_results: $1+\omega=-\omega^2$ and $1+\omega^2=-\omega$, so $(1+\omega)^n=(-1)^n\omega^{2n}$.
The representation $A+B\omega+C\omega^2$ is not unique: $(A,B,C)$ can be shifted by $(k,k,k)$. The quantity $3A-2B-C$ is shift-invariant because $3-2-1=0$, which is why the answer is well defined.
$\sum_{k\equiv r\,(\mathrm{mod}\,3)}\binom7k$ gives the coefficients: $43,\ 43,\ 42$ (they add up to $2^7=128$).

concepts: Circle and inversion in the complex plane
questions.question: Let the complex numbers $\alpha$ and $\frac1{\bar\alpha}$ lie on the circles $|z-z_0|^2=4$ and $|z-z_0|^2=16$ respectively, where $z_0=1+i$. Then the value of $100|\alpha|^2$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: The cross term $\alpha\bar z_0+\bar\alpha z_0$ appears in both circle equations (scaled by $|\alpha|^2$); eliminate it.
solution: $|\alpha-z_0|^2=4$: $(\alpha-z_0)(\bar\alpha-\bar z_0)=4$, so $|\alpha|^2-\alpha\bar z_0-\bar\alpha z_0+|z_0|^2=4$. With $|z_0|^2=2$: $|\alpha|^2-(\alpha\bar z_0+\bar\alpha z_0)=2$ ... (i).
Expand: $1-(\alpha\bar z_0+\bar\alpha z_0)+|\alpha|^2|z_0|^2=16|\alpha|^2$, i.e. $1-(\alpha\bar z_0+\bar\alpha z_0)+2|\alpha|^2=16|\alpha|^2$ ... (ii).

Remark: this is the value the key expects, but the data are inconsistent - a point $\alpha$ with $|\alpha-z_0|=2$ and $|z_0|=\sqrt2$ must have $|\alpha|\ge2-\sqrt2\approx0.59$, while $|\alpha|^2=\frac15$ gives $|\alpha|\approx0.45$, so no complex $\alpha$ lies on both circles.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use polar form $\alpha=re^{i\theta}$; the point $\frac1{\bar\alpha}=\frac1re^{i\theta}$ has the same direction, and the angle enters both equations only through one cosine, which is eliminated.

useful_results: $|z-z_0|^2=|z|^2-2\,\mathrm{Re}(z\bar z_0)+|z_0|^2$; the point $\frac1{\bar\alpha}$ is the inverse of $\alpha$ in the unit circle: same ray from $0$, modulus $\frac1{|\alpha|}$, so its cross term is the original divided by $|\alpha|^2$.
When two conditions share one awkward quantity (here $\mathrm{Re}(\alpha\bar z_0)$), eliminate it between them instead of solving for it.
Instance: with $|z_0|^2=2$ the system collapses to $3+|\alpha|^2=16|\alpha|^2$; the general form is $1-(|\alpha|^2-d_1+|z_0|^2)+|z_0|^2|\alpha|^2=d_2|\alpha|^2$ for radii$^2$ $d_1,d_2$.

concepts: Complex roots of a quadratic and reduction of powers
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2-x+2=0$ with $\mathrm{Im}(\alpha)>\mathrm{Im}(\beta)$. Then $\alpha^6+\alpha^4+\beta^4-5\alpha^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Reduce $x^6$ to $5x^2+12$ using $x^2+2=x$; then only $\alpha^4+\beta^4$ remains and it is symmetric.
solution: The expression $=12+1=13$. (The condition $\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha>\mathrm{Im}\,\beta$ is not needed: the result holds for either root.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Reduce every power to a linear polynomial in $x$ using $x^2=x-2$, then use $\alpha+\beta=1$.

useful_results: Every power of a root of $x^2=px-q$ reduces to the form $ax+b$ (division by the quadratic); symmetric expressions then need only $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$.
An asymmetric piece like $\alpha^6-5\alpha^2$ may be a constant ($12$) for either root, so the ordering condition $\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha>\mathrm{Im}\,\beta$ can be a red herring.

concepts: Polar form and powers of complex numbers
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2-\sqrt6x+3=0$ such that $\mathrm{Im}(\alpha)>\mathrm{Im}(\beta)$. Let $a,b$ be integers not divisible by $3$ and $n$ be a natural number such that $\frac{\alpha^{99}}{\beta}+\alpha^{98}=3^n(a+ib)$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Then $n+a+b$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Factor $\alpha^{98}\left(\frac\alpha\beta+1\right)$ and use $\alpha=\sqrt3e^{i\pi/4}$, $\beta=\sqrt3e^{-i\pi/4}$.
solution: $\alpha=\sqrt3e^{i\pi/4}$ and $\beta=\sqrt3e^{-i\pi/4}$ (the root with positive imaginary part is $\alpha$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $\alpha\beta=3$ and $\alpha^2=3i$, we get $\frac\alpha\beta=i$ and $\alpha^{98}=(3i)^{49}$ with no trigonometry.

useful_results: For a quadratic $x^2-px+q$ with complex conjugate roots: $\frac\alpha\beta=\frac{\alpha^2}{q}$, which is a unit complex number; here $\frac\alpha\beta=i$ and $\alpha^2=3i$.
Powers of $i$ cycle with period $4$: $i^{49}=i$. Reduce the exponent of $e^{i\theta}$ modulo $2\pi$ (or of $i$ modulo $4$) before evaluating.
Uniqueness: $3^n(a+ib)$ with $3\nmid a,b$ is a unique form, because $3^n$ is the largest power of $3$ dividing both parts.

concepts: Modulus and argument of complex numbers
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: If $\alpha$ denotes the number of solutions of $|1-i|^x=2^x$ and $\beta=\left(\frac{|z|}{\arg(z)}\right)$, where $z=\frac\pi4(1+i)^4\left[\frac{1-\sqrt\pi i}{\sqrt\pi+i}+\frac{\sqrt\pi-i}{1+\sqrt\pi i}\right]$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$, then the distance of the point $(\alpha,\beta)$ from the line $4x-3y=7$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Simplify the bracket to $-2i$ and $(1+i)^4$ to $-4$; then $z=2\pi i$, $|z|=2\pi$, $\arg z=\frac\pi2$.
solution: The point is $(1,4)$; its distance from $4x-3y-7=0$ is $\frac{|4-12-7|}{\sqrt{16+9}}=\frac{15}{5}=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Spot the factorisations $1-\sqrt\pi i=-i(\sqrt\pi+i)$ and $\sqrt\pi-i=-i(1+\sqrt\pi i)$: each fraction is simply $-i$.
solution: $-i(\sqrt\pi+i)=-\sqrt\pi i+1=1-\sqrt\pi i$, so the first fraction is $-i$.
$-i(1+\sqrt\pi i)=-i+\sqrt\pi=\sqrt\pi-i$, so the second fraction is $-i$.
The bracket is $-2i$ and $z=\frac\pi4(-4)(-2i)=2\pi i$, giving $\beta=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/2}=4$; also $\alpha=1$ as before.

useful_results: $\frac{1-ai}{a+i}=-i$ for every real $a$ (since $1-ai=-i(a+i)$) and $\frac{a-i}{1+ai}=-i$: look for a factor $\pm i$ before rationalising.
Distance from $(x_0,y_0)$ to $ax+by+c=0$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$; the equation $c^x=d^x$ with $c\ne d$ has only $x=0$.

concepts: Regions in the complex plane
Maximum and minimum distance from a point
questions.question: Let $P=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z+2-3i|\le1\}$ and $Q=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:z(1+i)+\bar z(1-i)\le-8\right\}$. Let in $P\cap Q$, $|z-3+2i|$ be maximum and minimum at $z_1$ and $z_2$ respectively. If $|z_1|^2+2|z_2|^2=\alpha+\beta\sqrt2$, where $\alpha,\beta$ are integers, then $\alpha+\beta$ equals ______.
questions.key_idea: $|z-3+2i|$ is the distance from $T=3-2i$; $T$ lies on the line through the disc's centre perpendicular to the cutting line, so both extreme points are easy to place.
solution: $P$: the disc with centre $c=(-2,3)$ and radius $1$.
$|z-3+2i|$ is the distance from $T=(3,-2)$. $T$ and $c$ both satisfy $x+y-1=0$ ($L_1$), which is perpendicular to $L_2$.
The centre satisfies $x-y+4=-1\le0$ and its distance from $L_2$ is $\frac1{\sqrt2}<1$: $P\cap Q$ is the part of the disc on the centre's side of $L_2$ (the larger cap).
Maximum: the farthest point of the disc from $T$ lies on $L_1$ beyond $c$: $z_1=\left(-2-\frac1{\sqrt2},\,3+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)$; it satisfies $x-y+4=-2.4<0$, so it is in $Q$.

Minimum: the nearest point of the disc to $T$ is $\left(-2+\frac1{\sqrt2},3-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)$ but $x-y+4=0.41>0$, so it is cut off. The nearest point of the cap is then on the chord: the foot of the perpendicular from $T$ to $L_2$, which is $L_1\cap L_2$ (as $L_1\perp L_2$): $z_2=\left(-\frac32,\frac52\right)$, inside the disc.

alternate_solutions.idea: Locate the extremes with vector formulas: farthest point $=c+\frac{c-T}{|c-T|}r$, nearest point of the chord $=$ foot of the perpendicular from $T$ to $L_2$.
solution: Foot of the perpendicular from $T$ to $x-y+4=0$: $T-\frac{3-(-2)+4}{2}(1,-1)=(3,-2)-\frac92(1,-1)=\left(-\frac32,\frac52\right)=z_2$.
$z_2$ is at distance $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}<1$ from $c$, so it lies in $P$, and it satisfies the boundary of $Q$; it is the minimum because the unconstrained nearest point of $P$ to $T$ is cut off by $Q$.

useful_results: Extreme distances from a point $T$ to a disc (centre $c$, radius $r$): $|T-c|\pm r$ along the line $Tc$; if a half-plane cuts off the nearest point, the minimum moves to the chord (perpendicular foot if it lies inside the disc, otherwise a chord end).
$z(1+i)+\bar z(1-i)=2\mathrm{Re}[(1+i)z]=2(x-y)$: in general $\bar pz+p\bar z=2\mathrm{Re}(\bar pz)$ is a real linear form, so $\bar pz+p\bar z\le k$ is a half-plane.
Perpendicular lines through the same point make the 'foot of the perpendicular' coincide with an intersection point - check for such coincidences before computing.

concepts: Equation involving $\bar z^2$ and $|z|$
questions.question: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the sum and the product of all the non-zero solutions of the equation $(\bar z)^2+|z|=0$, $z\in\mathbb{C}$. Then $4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Separate real and imaginary parts: $xy=0$ leaves two cases, giving $z=\pm i$.
solution: Case $x=0$: $-y^2+|y|=0$, i.e. $|y|(1-|y|)=0$, so $y=0$ or $y=\pm1$; the non-zero solutions are $z=i$ and $z=-i$.
Case $y=0$: $x^2+|x|=0$ forces $x=0$, i.e. only $z=0$, which is excluded.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take moduli of $\bar z^2=-|z|$: $|z|^2=|z|$, so a non-zero solution has $|z|=1$ and $\bar z^2=-1$.
solution: Then $\bar z^2=-1$, so $\bar z=\pm i$ and $z=\mp i$.
Check: $(\bar z)^2=-1$ and $|z|=1$ sum to $0$ ✓. The solutions $i,-i$ give $\alpha=0$, $\beta=1$ and $4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)=4$: option (C).

useful_results: $\bar z^{\,2}=-|z|$ has a negative real right side, so $\bar z^{\,2}$ must be a negative real number: $\bar z$ is purely imaginary; the modulus equation then fixes $|z|=1$.
For $z^n=r|z|^m$ type equations: take moduli first; then the equation reduces to a root-of-unity problem.
Sum and product of the non-zero roots here use only the list $\{i,-i\}$ (not a polynomial's coefficients).

concepts: Regions in the complex plane
Area of a sector
questions.question: The area (in sq. units) of the region $S=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-1|\le2;\ (z+\bar z)+i(z-\bar z)\le2,\ \mathrm{Im}(z)\ge0\right\}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Both lines pass through the centre $(1,0)$ of the disc, so $S$ is a sector; read its angle from the two lines.
solution: $|z-1|\le2$: the disc with centre $(1,0)$ and radius $2$.
$(z+\bar z)+i(z-\bar z)=2x+i(2iy)=2x-2y\le2$, i.e. $x-y\le1$; the boundary $y=x-1$ passes through the centre $(1,0)$.
Measure the angle $\varphi$ at the centre $(1,0)$: $y\ge0$ means $\varphi\in[0,\pi]$; $x-1\le y$ means $\cos\varphi\le\sin\varphi$, i.e. $\varphi\in\left[\frac\pi4,\frac{5\pi}{4}\right]$.
The intersection is $\varphi\in\left[\frac\pi4,\pi\right]$: a sector of angle $\frac{3\pi}{4}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Start from the upper half-disc (area $2\pi$) and subtract the sector cut off by the line $y=x-1$.
solution: The part of it with $x-y>1$ (below the line $y=x-1$) is the sector between the directions $0$ and $\frac\pi4$ at the centre: area $\frac12\cdot4\cdot\frac\pi4=\frac\pi2$.

useful_results: A line through the centre of a disc divides it into two equal halves; two lines through the centre cut out a sector, so $\mathrm{Area}=\frac12r^2\theta$ with $\theta$ read from the line slopes.
$(z+\bar z)+i(z-\bar z)=2(x-y)$ and generally $p\bar z+\bar pz=2\mathrm{Re}(\bar pz)$ are real linear forms: they give half-planes.
Check each boundary line against the centre first (here $y=x-1$ at $x=1$: $y=0$ ✓ passes through the centre).

concepts: Triangle inequality and modulus of complex numbers
Conjugate and cyclic sums of complex fractions
questions.question:
Consider the following two statements.
Statement I: For any two non-zero complex numbers $z_1,z_2$: $\left(|z_1|+|z_2|\right)\left|\frac{z_1}{|z_1|}+\frac{z_2}{|z_2|}\right|\le2\left(|z_1|+|z_2|\right)$ and
Statement II: If $x,y,z$ are three distinct complex numbers and $a,b,c$ are three positive real numbers such that $\frac{a}{|y-z|}=\frac{b}{|z-x|}=\frac{c}{|x-y|}$, then $\frac{a^2}{y-z}+\frac{b^2}{z-x}+\frac{c^2}{x-y}=1$.\nBetween the above two statements:
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
questions.answer: (A) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
questions.key_idea: Statement I is the triangle inequality for two unit vectors; Statement II sums to $0$ because $\frac{a^2}{y-z}=k^2\,\overline{(y-z)}$.
solution: Multiplying by $|z_1|+|z_2|>0$ gives Statement I: it is correct.
Statement II: let the common ratio be $k>0$: $a=k|y-z|$, $b=k|z-x|$, $c=k|x-y|$.
$\frac{a^2}{y-z}=\frac{k^2|y-z|^2}{y-z}=\frac{k^2(y-z)\overline{(y-z)}}{y-z}=k^2(\bar y-\bar z)$; similarly $\frac{b^2}{z-x}=k^2(\bar z-\bar x)$ and $\frac{c^2}{x-y}=k^2(\bar x-\bar y)$.
The sum is $k^2\left[(\bar y-\bar z)+(\bar z-\bar x)+(\bar x-\bar y)\right]=0\neq1$.
So Statement II is incorrect: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Check Statement I with the parallelogram law and refute Statement II by one numerical example.
solution: For unit vectors $u_1,u_2$: $|u_1+u_2|^2+|u_1-u_2|^2=2+2=4$, so $|u_1+u_2|^2=4-|u_1-u_2|^2\le4$ and $|u_1+u_2|\le2$; multiply by $|z_1|+|z_2|$: Statement I holds.
Statement II: take $x=0,\ y=1,\ z=i$ and $k=1$: $a=|y-z|=\sqrt2$, $b=|z-x|=1$, $c=|x-y|=1$.
A single counter-example shows Statement II is false; I is true: option (A).

useful_results: Cyclic sums of differences vanish: $(y-z)+(z-x)+(x-y)=0$. After rewriting $\frac{|w|^2}{w}=\bar w$, such sums collapse to $0$ - this is why a claimed value $1$ is suspect.
$|u_1+u_2|\le|u_1|+|u_2|$ with equality iff $u_1,u_2$ point in the same direction; for unit vectors $|u_1+u_2|=2\left|\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\right|\le2$.
When a statement claims an identity for all inputs, one numerical counter-example (with easy numbers like $0,1,i$) settles it.

concepts: Regions in the complex plane
Area of a sector
questions.question: Let $S_1=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|\le5\}$, $S_2=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Im}\left(\frac{z+1-\sqrt3i}{1-\sqrt3i}\right)\ge0\right\}$ and $S_3=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}(z)\ge0\}$. Then the area of the region $S_1\cap S_2\cap S_3$ is:
questions.key_idea: $S_2$ is a half-plane bounded by a line through the origin, so the region is a sector of the disc of radius $5$.
solution: Its imaginary part has numerator $\sqrt3(x+1)+(y-\sqrt3)=\sqrt3x+y$, so $S_2$ is $\sqrt3x+y\ge0$ (the line has slope $-\sqrt3$ and passes through the origin).

In polar angle $\varphi$: $x\ge0$ gives $\varphi\in\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$; $\sqrt3x+y\ge0$ gives $\varphi\in\left[-\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right]$. The intersection is $\varphi\in\left[-\frac\pi3,\frac\pi2\right]$, of angle $\frac{5\pi}{6}$.
Area $=\frac12\cdot5^2\cdot\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac{125\pi}{12}$ (equivalently a quarter disc $\frac{25\pi}{4}$ plus a sector $\frac{25\pi}{6}$): option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Start from the half-disc $x\ge0$ (area $\frac{25\pi}{2}$) and subtract the wedge cut off by $\sqrt3x+y<0$.
solution: $S_1\cap S_3$ is a half-disc of area $\frac12\pi\cdot25=\frac{25\pi}{2}$.
The part with $\sqrt3x+y<0$ and $x\ge0$ lies between the directions $\varphi=-\frac\pi2$ and $\varphi=-\frac\pi3$: a wedge of angle $\frac\pi6$.

useful_results: $\mathrm{Im}\frac{z-a}{b}\ge0$ is the half-plane to the left of the directed line through $a$ with direction $b$; if $a$ is a real multiple of $b$ the line passes through the origin (here $a=-1+\sqrt3i=-b$).
A region of a disc bounded by lines through the centre is a sector: area $=\frac12r^2\theta$, with $\theta$ from the line angles ($y=-\sqrt3x$ is at $-60^\circ$).
Quick check on pieces: $\frac{25\pi}{4}+\frac{25\pi}{6}=\frac{75\pi+50\pi}{12}=\frac{125\pi}{12}$.

concepts: Modulus identity for two complex numbers
questions.question: If $z_1,z_2$ are two distinct complex numbers such that $\left|\frac{z_1-2z_2}{\frac12-z_1\bar z_2}\right|=2$, then:
options: both $z_1$ and $z_2$ lie on the same circle
$z_1$ lies on a circle of radius $\frac12$ and $z_2$ lies on a circle of radius $1$
either $z_1$ lies on a circle of radius $1$ or $z_2$ lies on a circle of radius $\frac12$
either $z_1$ lies on a circle of radius $\frac12$ or $z_2$ lies on a circle of radius $1$
questions.answer: (C) either $z_1$ lies on a circle of radius $1$ or $z_2$ lies on a circle of radius $\frac12$
questions.key_idea: Square both sides; the cross terms cancel and the equation factorises as $\left(|z_1|^2-1\right)\left(1-4|z_2|^2\right)=0$.
solution: So $|z_1|=1$ or $|z_2|=\frac12$: either $z_1$ lies on a circle of radius $1$ or $z_2$ lies on a circle of radius $\frac12$: option (C).
questions.correction_note: Typo in the PDF: in the expansion of $|z_1-2z_2|^2$ its first term is printed as $|z_2|^2$; it should be $|z_1|^2$ (the next lines use the right quantity). Corrected; the answer (C) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the identity $\left|1-a\bar b\right|^2-|a-b|^2=(1-|a|^2)(1-|b|^2)$ with $a=z_1$, $b=2z_2$.
solution: The condition says $|z_1-2z_2|=|1-2z_1\bar z_2|$, i.e. $|a-b|=|1-a\bar b|$ with $a=z_1$, $b=2z_2$.

useful_results: $|1-a\bar b|^2-|a-b|^2=(1-|a|^2)(1-|b|^2)$ for all complex $a,b$ (check: $a=\frac12$, $b=\frac13$ gives $\frac{25}{36}-\frac1{36}=\frac23=\frac34\cdot\frac89$).
Consequences: $|a-b|=|1-a\bar b|$ iff $|a|=1$ or $|b|=1$; if $|a|,|b|<1$ then $|a-b|<|1-a\bar b|$ (the Blaschke / disc-automorphism inequality).
Rescale to fit the identity: here $b=2z_2$ turns $|b|=1$ into $|z_2|=\frac12$.

concepts: Unit circle parametrisation of $z+2$
questions.question: Let $z$ be a complex number such that $|z+2|=1$ and $\mathrm{Im}\left(\frac{z+1}{z+2}\right)=\frac15$. Then the value of $\left|\mathrm{Re}(z+2)\right|$ is:
questions.key_idea: Put $z+2=e^{i\theta}$: then $\frac{z+1}{z+2}=1-e^{-i\theta}$ and its imaginary part is $\sin\theta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: On the unit circle $\frac1w=\bar w$, so $\frac{z+1}{z+2}=1-\overline{(z+2)}$ and its imaginary part equals $\mathrm{Im}(z+2)$.

useful_results: If $|w|=1$ then $\frac1w=\bar w$; hence $\frac{w-1}{w}=1-\bar w$ and $\mathrm{Im}\frac{w-1}{w}=\mathrm{Im}\,w$, $\mathrm{Re}\frac{w-1}{w}=1-\mathrm{Re}\,w$.
On the unit circle $(\mathrm{Re}\,w)^2+(\mathrm{Im}\,w)^2=1$, so knowing one part gives the other up to sign - that is why the question asks for $|\mathrm{Re}|$.
Shifted unit circles $|z+2|=1$: set $w=z+2$ first and express every given quantity in $w$.

concepts: Powers of $i$
Number of positive integer solutions of a linear equation
questions.question: If the set $R=\{(a,b):a+5b=42,\ a,b\in\mathbb{N}\}$ has $m$ elements and $\sum_{n=1}^{m}\left(1-i^{n!}\right)=x+iy$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$, then the value of $m+x+y$ is:
questions.key_idea: $i^{n!}=1$ for $n\ge4$ (as $4\mid n!$), so only $n=1,2,3$ contribute to the sum.
solution: For $n\ge4$, $4\mid n!$, so $i^{n!}=1$ and the term $1-i^{n!}=0$.
useful_results: For $n\ge4$ the factorial $n!$ is a multiple of $4$, so $i^{n!}=1$; only a few initial terms of such a sum survive. Likewise $\omega^{n!}=1$ for $n\ge3$.
Number of positive solutions of $a+5b=N$: $\left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{5}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{41}{5}\right\rfloor=8$ (or list $a\equiv2\pmod5$: $2,7,\dots,37$).
$i^k$ depends only on $k\bmod4$: $1,i,-1,-i$ for $k\equiv0,1,2,3$.

concepts: Purely imaginary complex number
Trigonometric equations
questions.question: The sum of all possible values of $\theta\in[-\pi,2\pi]$, for which $\frac{1+i\cos\theta}{1-2i\cos\theta}$ is purely imaginary, is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Rationalise: the real part is $\frac{1-2\cos^2\theta}{1+4\cos^2\theta}$, which vanishes when $\cos^2\theta=\frac12$.
solution: Purely imaginary: real part $0$, i.e. $\cos^2\theta=\frac12$ (then $\cos\theta=\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}\neq0$, so the imaginary part is non-zero).

alternate_solutions.idea: The condition depends on $\cos^2\theta$, which is even, so roots in $[-\pi,\pi]$ cancel in pairs $\pm\theta$ and only the roots in $(\pi,2\pi]$ remain.
solution: $\cos^2\theta=\frac12$ is unchanged by $\theta\mapsto-\theta$, so the solutions in $[-\pi,\pi]$ come in pairs $\pm\theta$ with sum $0$ (there are four, none equal to $0$).
The remaining interval $(\pi,2\pi]$ contains $\theta=\frac{5\pi}{4}$ and $\frac{7\pi}{4}$ (the solutions of $\cos2\theta=0$ there).

useful_results: $\frac{1+ia}{1-ib}$ has real part $\frac{1-ab}{1+b^2}$ and imaginary part $\frac{a+b}{1+b^2}$; with $a=\cos\theta$, $b=2\cos\theta$ the real part is $\frac{1-2\cos^2\theta}{1+4\cos^2\theta}$.
For conditions in $\cos^2\theta$ (or $\cos2\theta$) the solution set is symmetric in $\theta\to-\theta$ and in $\theta\to\pi-\theta$: sums over symmetric intervals cancel in pairs.
The solutions of $\cos2\theta=0$ are $\theta=\frac\pi4+\frac{k\pi}{2}$; list the ones inside the given interval carefully (here $[-\pi,2\pi]$ gives six).

concepts: Purely imaginary quotient (circle locus)
Maximum distance from a point to a circle
questions.question: Let $z$ be a complex number such that the real part of $\frac{z-2i}{z+2i}$ is zero. Then, the maximum value of $|z-(6+8i)|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Real part zero means $\frac{z-2i}{z+2i}+\overline{\left(\frac{z-2i}{z+2i}\right)}=0$, which simplifies to $|z|=2$; then use distance to centre plus radius.
solution: So $|z|=2$: a circle with centre $0$ and radius $2$ (the point $-2i$ is excluded).
The distance from the centre $0$ to the point $6+8i$ is $10$.
The maximum of $|z-(6+8i)|$ over the circle is $10+2=12$ (attained at $z=-\frac{6+8i}{5}$, which is allowed): option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: A purely imaginary $\frac{z-a}{z-b}$ means the angle at $z$ subtended by $a,b$ is a right angle: $z$ is on the circle with diameter $2i,-2i$.
solution: $\frac{z-2i}{z+2i}$ is purely imaginary (real part $0$) exactly when $\angle(2i,z,-2i)=90^\circ$ (Thales).
So $z$ lies on the circle with diameter from $-2i$ to $2i$: centre $0$, radius $2$.
Farthest point of this circle from $P=6+8i$: along the line from $P$ through the centre, at distance $|P|+2=10+2=12$: option (D).

useful_results: $\mathrm{Re}\frac{z-a}{z-b}=0\iff z$ lies on the circle with diameter $ab$ (Thales); $\mathrm{Im}\frac{z-a}{z-b}=0\iff z$ lies on the line $ab$.
Distance from an external point $P$ to a circle (centre $C$, radius $r$): maximum $|PC|+r$, minimum $|PC|-r$.
Check that the extremal point is not one of the excluded points ($z=-2i$ here): the maximiser $-\frac{6+8i}{5}$ is different.

concepts: Roots of a polynomial and symmetric products
Modulus of complex numbers
questions.question: Let $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ be the solutions of the equation $4x^4+8x^3-17x^2-12x+9=0$ and $\left(4+x_1^2\right)\left(4+x_2^2\right)\left(4+x_3^2\right)\left(4+x_4^2\right)=\frac{125}{16}m$. Then the value of $m$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Write $4+x^2=(x-2i)(x+2i)$, so the product is $\frac{P(2i)P(-2i)}{16}=\frac{|P(2i)|^2}{16}$.
solution: $P$ has real coefficients, so $P(-2i)=\overline{P(2i)}$, and $\prod(4+x_k^2)=\frac{|P(2i)|^2}{16}$ - valid whether the roots are real or not.

alternate_solutions.idea: Factorise the quartic: it has four rational roots, so the product can be computed directly.
solution: $P(x)=(2x-3)(x+3)(2x-1)(x+1)$; the roots are $\frac32,\ -3,\ \frac12,\ -1$ (check: product of the constants $-3\cdot3\cdot(-1)\cdot1=9$ ✓).

useful_results: For real-coefficient $P$ of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $a_n$: $\prod(x_k^2+a^2)=\frac{P(ia)P(-ia)}{a_n^2}=\frac{|P(ia)|^2}{a_n^2}$ - true for all roots, real or complex.
Similarly $\prod(x_k-t)=(-1)^n\frac{P(t)}{a_n}$ and $\prod(x_k^2-t^2)=\frac{P(t)P(-t)}{a_n^2}$.
Instance check: the roots $\frac32,-3,\frac12,-1$ give $\frac{25}{4}\cdot13\cdot\frac{17}{4}\cdot5=\frac{27625}{16}$, matching $\frac{|141-88i|^2}{16}$.

concepts: Lattice points in a region of the complex plane
Modulus of a complex number
questions.question: The sum of the square of the modulus of the elements in the set $\{z=a+ib:\ a,b\in\mathbb{Z},\ z\in\mathbb{C},\ |z-1|\le1,\ |z-5|\le|z-5i|\}$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Only five lattice points lie in $|z-1|\le1$; test the second condition ($a\ge b$) on each.
useful_results: $|z-p|\le|z-q|$ is the closed half-plane on $p$'s side of the perpendicular bisector of $pq$; for $p=5$, $q=5i$ the bisector is $y=x$ and the half-plane is $a\ge b$.
Lattice points in a disc of radius $1$ about an integer centre: the centre and its four neighbours (axis steps only, since $\sqrt2>1$).
For such small counts do not draw: list the candidate lattice points and test every condition on each.
